title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

deep.reconstruction:
Setting and problem. The page continues a method for finding the Moon's node and the inclination of its orbit from the timed contacts of a lunar eclipse. The geometry is a small spherical triangle at the node ☊:
- one side runs along the ecliptic to the shadow centre;
- one side runs along the lunar orbit to the Moon's centre;
- the angle at the node is the inclination ρ;
- the side opposite ρ is the centre-to-centre distance.

Notation (from the previous page):
- x = ☊σ is the distance of the shadow centre from the node at mid-eclipse.
- At mid-eclipse the Moon stands at x−c along its orbit, where c = (m+n+2k) sin2x tan²(ρ/2)/(g(n−m)) is a small arc (in seconds; g = 1″ in radians).
- The partial phase (first and last contact, separation f = α+β, duration h) gives the half-motions a = ½h(n+k) for the Moon and b = ½h(m+k) for the shadow.
- The total phase (immersion and emersion, separation F = α−β, duration H) gives A and B in the same way.

Key identity. By the spherical law of cosines, with P = x−c∓a and Q = x∓b:
cos f = cosP cosQ + sinP sinQ cosρ = cos²(ρ/2) cos(P−Q) + sin²(ρ/2) cos(P+Q).
At first contact this reads cos f = cos²(ρ/2) cos(a−b+c) + sin²(ρ/2) cos(2x−a−b−c). Hence sin²(ρ/2) = (cos(a−b+c)−cos f)/(cos(a−b+c)−cos(2x−a−b−c)).

Top of the page. The same relation holds for the total phase. Equating the two expressions eliminates ρ (up to its weak presence through c) and gives a transcendental equation for x. Euler judges it harder to solve than his earlier iterative method.

§21: full elimination of ρ and c. Write first contact, last contact (P = x−c+a, Q = x+b), and their sum and difference, linearised in the small c. Put T = tan²(ρ/2).
- Difference: c sin(a−b) = T sin(a+b)(sin2x − c cos2x).
- Sum: T(cos f − cos(a+b)(cos2x + c sin2x)) = cos(a−b) − cos f.
- Eliminating T gives c = (cos(a−b)−cos f) sin(a+b) sin2x / [cos f sin(a−b) + sin2b cos2x − cos f sin(a+b) cos2x]. Euler's denominator is reproduced exactly.
- Equating this c with the corresponding total-phase c gives a relation linear in cos2x: u(P'R−PR') = P'Q−PQ'.
- Substituting cos2x = (1−tan²x)/(1+tan²x) yields exactly Euler's printed numerator/denominator. So the left-hand side is tan²x.
- T then follows from the first-contact equation linearised in c. Both printed forms of tan²(ρ/2) check, using cos(2x−a−b−c) ≈ cos(2x−a−b) + c sin(2x−a−b).

Euler warns that the complicated formulas are ill-conditioned with respect to small observational errors. He advises using the earlier formulas instead.

§22: time of true opposition. Let opposition occur z hours after mid-eclipse.
- The shadow is then at x + z(m+k)″ from the node.
- The Moon is at x − c + z(n+k)″ along its orbit.
- Equal longitudes means the right spherical triangle relation tan(ecliptic arc) = cosρ · tan(orbit arc). Hence cosρ = tan(x+z(m+k)″)/tan(x−c+z(n+k)″), expanded with the tangent addition formula.
- The next page linearises this to z ≈ 2(n+k) sin2x tan²(ρ/2)/(g(n−m)²) hours: the classical reduction from mid-eclipse to opposition.
errors: The equation for x in §21 is printed/transcribed as 'tang 2x = ...'. Re-deriving it (equate the two phase-wise expressions for c, which is linear in cos2x, then use cos2x = (1−tan²x)/(1+tan²x)) gives Euler's numerator and denominator exactly for tan²x, not tan 2x. Either the print reads tang²x and the transcription dropped the superscript, or the 1862 print/manuscript carries a misprint. Mathematically the left side must be tan²x.

Formula for c in §21: the numerator should be (cos(a−b) − cos f) sin(a+b) sin2x, not (cos f − cos(a−b)) sin(a+b) sin2x. With a > b and f > a−b (so cos(a−b) > cos f), the printed sign makes c negative for sin2x > 0. That contradicts the definition c = (m+n+2k) sin2x tan²(ρ/2)/(g(n−m)) > 0. The denominator is correct. The sign slip does not affect the tan²x formula, which is invariant under flipping both phase c-numerators.
The §21 formulas are first-order in the small arc c (cos c ≈ 1, sin c ≈ c, c² dropped), although Euler presents them as the result of exact elimination.

The four contact equations overdetermine the three unknowns x, ρ, c, because a:b = A:B. Euler eliminates T = tan²(ρ/2) separately within each phase and equates the two c's. Equality of the two phase-wise T's is not enforced; it serves only as an implicit check.
In §22 'Sit brevitatis gratia c = ... g(n+m)' should be g(n−m), consistent with the previous page and with the use of c on the next page (likely a transcription/print slip).

ideas.what: Writing the spherical cosine law for the eclipse triangle as cos f = cos²(ρ/2)cos(P−Q) + sin²(ρ/2)cos(P+Q), so that the small inclination enters weakly, and deriving sin²(ρ/2) and tan²(ρ/2) formulas
ideas.modern_name: half-angle form of the spherical law of cosines; reduction of eclipse contact geometry
ideas.where_published: E838 (Opera postuma 1862); similar trigonometric manipulations appear throughout Euler's astronomical papers

ideas.what: Determining both the node longitude and the inclination from the times of the four contacts (partial and total) of a single total lunar eclipse, by eliminating ρ and c to get a closed formula for x
ideas.modern_name: determination of lunar orbital elements (node, inclination) from eclipse contact timings
ideas.usually_credited_to: eclipse-based node determination goes back to Hipparchus/Ptolemy; analytic contact-time reductions to 18th-century astronomers (e.g. Mayer, Lalande)
ideas.where_published: E838 only, as far as known

ideas.what: Explicit warning that the closed-form elimination is numerically ill-conditioned (small observation errors strongly distort the result), with a preference for an iterative method
ideas.usually_credited_to: general practice; error analysis formalised later (Gauss, Legendre)

ideas.what: Condition of true opposition: tan(ecliptic arc) = cosρ · tan(orbit arc), leading to the reduction of mid-eclipse time to opposition time
ideas.modern_name: reduction to the ecliptic; correction from middle of eclipse to opposition
ideas.usually_credited_to: classical spherical astronomy (standard in 18th-century eclipse calculation)
ideas.where_published: E838; the reduction is standard in contemporary astronomy texts

missed.claim: The §21 closed formula is for tan²x, not tan 2x: it follows exactly from equating the two phase-wise expressions for c (a relation linear in cos2x) and substituting cos2x = (1−tan²x)/(1+tan²x). Also, the numerator of the c-formula has the wrong sign. Anyone using the Opera postuma text (or its transcription) as printed/read would get wrong node positions.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: A textual/mathematical correction to the posthumous edition and its transcription, relevant to any edition or commentary of E838. Not a new mathematical result.

deep.surprise_reason: Routine spherical-trigonometric reduction of eclipse observations; the only notable findings are a verified misprint or misreading (tan²x vs tan 2x) and a sign slip in the c-formula, plus Euler's sensible remark on ill-conditioning.
transcription_corrections: §21: 'tang 2x =' should be 'tang² x =' (tan²x); the derivation reproduces Euler's numerator and denominator exactly for tan²x. Whether the superscript is in the scan is unclear (left margin is darkened).
§22: 'c = ... / g(n+m)[?]' should read g(n−m), consistent with the preceding line and the next page.
§21 c-formula: as printed the numerator is (cos f − cos(a−b)); the mathematically correct numerator is (cos(a−b) − cos f). This is an error in the source, not the transcription.
